report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is **not supported by available evidence**. Apples naturally make a protective wax; post-harvest washing can remove it, so packers may apply a very small edible coating to reduce moisture loss and preserve quality. In the U.S., FDA policy permits fruit/vegetable coatings only when their components are authorized food additives, GRAS substances, or otherwise permitted for that use.  
https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cpg-sec-562550-safety-and-labeling-waxed-coated-fruits-and-vegetables

One common coating is carnauba wax (E903), a plant-derived glazing agent. EFSA’s 2012 re-evaluation did identify an *evidence gap*: no chronic-toxicity or carcinogenicity studies were available, so it did not set a numerical acceptable daily intake. That is not evidence that the wax causes cancer; it means long-term data were insufficient for that particular quantitative assessment.  
https://ucrisportal.univie.ac.at/en/publications/scientific-opinion-on-the-re-evaluation-of-carnauba-wax-e-903-as-a/

Other edible coatings may include shellac (E904). EFSA’s 2024 assessment concluded that a conservatively calculated exceedance of its ADI for relevant shellac did **not** indicate a safety concern.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11292212/

Thus, concern is understandable—“food-grade” does not mean every compound has unlimited data—but the evidence does not establish apple wax coatings as carcinogenic. This conclusion applies to regulated edible coatings, not non-food waxes or contamination from unrelated chemicals. Washing apples under running water can remove dirt and some surface residue, but peeling is unnecessary for cancer prevention based on current evidence.
